cls: Live attenuated Mycobacterium bovis (biological response modifier / vaccine)
pharm: Intravesical immunotherapy for bladder cancer; tuberculosis vaccine
quick: Intravesical: one instillation weekly for 6 weeks (induction)
Should not be used in pregnancy unless clearly needed
Not known if excreted in milk; use caution
No specific renal dose adjustment for intravesical use
Caution; granulomatous hepatitis can occur with dissemination
For systemic BCG infection, fever, cystitis, hematuria
summary: Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) is a live, attenuated strain of Mycobacterium bovis. Intravesical BCG (e.g., TICE BCG) is used to treat and prevent recurrence of carcinoma in situ (CIS) of the urinary bladder and to prevent recurrence of stage Ta/T1 papillary tumors after transurethral resection. As a vaccine it is used widely outside the US to prevent tuberculosis. Because it contains live mycobacteria, it can cause disseminated, potentially fatal BCG infection (BCG sepsis), and is contraindicated in immunosuppressed patients. The intravesical antineoplastic preparation and the TB immunizing preparation are different products and are not interchangeable.
indications: Intravesical treatment and prophylaxis of carcinoma in situ (CIS) of the urinary bladder
Prophylaxis of primary or recurrent stage Ta and/or T1 papillary bladder tumors after transurethral resection
Active immunization against tuberculosis (BCG vaccine, primarily outside the US)

dosage.d: One reconstituted dose (one vial/ampoule) instilled into the bladder once weekly for 6 weeks
dosage.n: May repeat the 6-week course once if no response and tumor remains

dosage.d: Instillations approximately monthly or per protocol (e.g., 3 weekly instillations at intervals over up to ~3 years)
dosage.n: Begin no sooner than 7-14 days after resection or traumatic catheterization

dosage.d: Single intradermal dose per the specific vaccine product label and national immunization schedule
dosage.n: Different product from intravesical BCG - not interchangeable

admin: Intravesical: instill into the empty bladder via catheter and retain for ~2 hours, with position changes; then void seated to avoid splashing
Reconstitute and handle aseptically using precautions for a live biological agent; treat as biohazard
Do NOT administer intravenously, subcutaneously or intramuscularly (intravesical use only)
Do not start within 7-14 days of transurethral resection, biopsy or traumatic catheterization (risk of systemic absorption)
Disinfect voided urine for ~6 hours after instillation (e.g., with bleach)
moa: BCG instilled into the bladder produces a local inflammatory and cell-mediated immune response in the bladder wall. Attachment of the organism to the urothelium triggers recruitment of immune cells and release of cytokines, generating an antitumor immune reaction. The precise mechanism is not fully defined. As a vaccine, BCG induces cell-mediated immunity that confers partial protection against tuberculous disease.

absolute: Immunosuppression or immunocompromise (congenital or acquired immunodeficiency, HIV/AIDS, leukemia, lymphoma)
Patients on immunosuppressive therapy, radiation or chemotherapy
Febrile illness or active urinary tract infection (intravesical)
Gross hematuria or recent traumatic catheterization (defer until resolved)
relative: Concurrent antibiotics with antimycobacterial activity (may impair efficacy)
monitor: Fever, malaise and flu-like symptoms suggesting systemic BCG infection
Severe or persistent cystitis, hematuria or symptoms beyond 2-3 days
Signs of disseminated infection (lung, liver, bone marrow)

preg: Should not be used during pregnancy unless clearly needed; defer elective intravesical treatment. Animal reproduction data are limited.
lact: It is not known whether BCG is excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions, exercise caution; consider deferring treatment or breastfeeding.
renal: No specific renal dose adjustment is described for intravesical use; ensure no active urinary tract infection before instillation.
hepatic: Granulomatous hepatitis can occur as part of disseminated BCG infection; monitor liver function if systemic reaction is suspected and treat with antituberculous therapy.

major: Immunosuppressants, corticosteroids, chemotherapy, radiation - impair the immune response and increase risk of disseminated infection; avoid
Antimicrobials active against M. bovis (e.g., fluoroquinolones, some antibiotics) - may reduce efficacy of intravesical BCG
moderate: Antituberculous drugs - used to TREAT BCG infection (isoniazid, rifampin); note BCG is resistant to pyrazinamide
Bone marrow suppressants - increase infection risk
interactions.food: Not applicable; instilled into the bladder or given as a vaccine.
interactions.diagnostics: BCG can cause conversion of the tuberculin (PPD) skin test to positive, complicating later TB testing.

serious: Disseminated BCG infection (BCG sepsis) - can be fatal
Granulomatous involvement of lung, liver, kidney, bone or prostate
Persistent high fever (>=39 C) or symptoms beyond 2-3 days
Severe local bladder reaction / contracted bladder
emergency: BCG sepsis / disseminated infection with high fever, rigors and hypotension

monitoring: Temperature and systemic symptoms after each instillation
Urinary symptoms - severity and duration of cystitis and hematuria
Signs of disseminated BCG infection (respiratory, hepatic, hematologic)
Bladder capacity and tumor response by cystoscopy per protocol
counsel: This treatment uses live bacteria; for about 6 hours after each instillation, sit to urinate and disinfect the toilet (e.g., with bleach) before flushing
Increase fluid intake after treatment to flush the bladder
Expect some burning, frequency and blood-tinged urine for a day or two
Seek urgent care for high fever, shaking chills, joint pain, persistent symptoms or feeling very unwell - these may signal a body-wide infection
Tell your doctor if you take steroids or have a weakened immune system
pk: Local immune response develops over hours to days after instillation
Inflammatory response peaks over days; antitumor effect over weeks of therapy
Not applicable - live organism, not a conventional drug
Immune effect persists; maintenance courses given over months to ~3 years
Refrigerate at 2-8 C, protect from light; reconstitute immediately before use
pearls: Intravesical antineoplastic BCG and the TB vaccine are different products and are NOT interchangeable
Contains live mycobacteria - never give to immunosuppressed patients; disseminated BCG infection can be fatal
Do not instill within 7-14 days of resection, biopsy or traumatic catheterization (systemic absorption risk)
Treat serious BCG infection with antituberculous therapy (isoniazid + rifampin) - BCG is resistant to pyrazinamide
Persistent high fever or symptoms beyond 2-3 days warrant evaluation for systemic BCG infection
BCG can convert the tuberculin (PPD) skin test to positive
missed: Intravesical instillations are scheduled by the urology team. A missed instillation should be rescheduled by the clinician; do not attempt to self-administer or double up. The dosing schedule is adjusted as needed.
overdose: Excess intravesical exposure or systemic absorption can cause disseminated BCG infection (BCG sepsis). Manage with prompt antituberculous therapy (e.g., isoniazid and rifampin), and consider corticosteroids in severe systemic reactions; provide supportive care. Seek infectious disease consultation.
